items.stem: Which of the following best explains why plastic pollution in the Pacific is a global political issue?
options: It only affects island states in the Pacific
It is a purely scientific question with no disagreement
Its causes and effects cross borders and require cooperation between states, firms and NGOs
It has already been solved by a binding UN treaty
items.answer: Its causes and effects cross borders and require cooperation between states, firms and NGOs
items.markingKey: C. Negotiations on a global plastics treaty (UNEP, from 2022) show multiple actors contesting rules across borders.

items.stem: Distinguish between a local political issue and a global political issue.
items.answer: A local issue affects a specific community and is decided mainly by local actors (e.g. a city zoning dispute), while a global issue crosses borders in its causes, effects or solutions and involves international actors (e.g. pandemic preparedness).
items.markingKey: A local issue affects a specific community and is decided mainly by local actors (e.g. a city zoning dispute), while a global issue crosses borders in its causes, effects or solutions and involves international actors (e.g. pandemic preparedness). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: "Global politics only studies relations between governments." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Global politics also studies non-state actors (NGOs, MNCs, social movements, individuals) and issues at local and individual levels, not just inter-state diplomacy.
items.markingKey: Global politics also studies non-state actors (NGOs, MNCs, social movements, individuals) and issues at local and individual levels, not just inter-state diplomacy. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Politics is not only what presidents do at summits. It is also the negotiation in a family over who works and who studies, and the decision of a village to resist a dam."
— Introductory lecture on global politics, university course reader (adapted)

Identify the view of politics presented in the source and explain one implication for how political issues are studied.
items.answer: The source presents a broad view of politics as power relations at every level, including the household and community; this implies analysts should study individual and local levels and non-state actors, not just states and leaders.
items.markingKey: The source presents a broad view of politics as power relations at every level, including the household and community; this implies analysts should study individual and local levels and non-state actors, not just states and leaders. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Using the Fridays for Future school strikes started by Greta Thunberg in 2018 as an example, explain how an individual can act at the global level.
items.answer: A single student's strike outside the Swedish parliament grew into coordinated global protests involving millions of young people in 2019. one individual's action at the local level scaled up through social media to influence global debate and agenda-setting on climate
items.markingKey: Context (A single student's strike outside the Swedish parliament grew into coordinated global protests involving millions of young people in 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: one individual's action at the local level scaled up through social media to influence global debate and agenda-setting on climate – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how an individual can act at the global level.

items.stem: Using one example you have studied, analyse how a single issue can be understood at the local, national and global levels of analysis.
items.answer: Strong answers choose a specific issue (e.g. Rana Plaza, Cochabamba water, plastic pollution), identify actors and power relations at each level, show how levels interact (e.g. global supply chain pressure → national regulation → local working conditions) and reach a judgement on which level offers most explanatory power.
items.markingKey: Strong answers choose a specific issue (e.g. Rana Plaza, Cochabamba water, plastic pollution), identify actors and power relations at each level, show how levels interact (e.g. global supply chain pressure → national regulation → local working conditions) and reach a judgement on which level offers most explanatory power.

items.stem: Which of the following political scientists defined politics as "who gets what, when, how"?
items.answer: Harold Lasswell
items.markingKey: B. Lasswell's 1936 book Politics: Who Gets What, When, How framed politics as the distribution of resources.

items.stem: Briefly explain why water access in a city can become a global political issue.
items.answer: Local water scarcity can be shaped by transnational actors and processes – foreign investors in privatised utilities, IMF loan conditions, climate change and cross-border rivers – so it links local grievances to global power structures (e.g. the 2000 Cochabamba water protests against a Bechtel-linked consortium).

(2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Rana Plaza factory collapse in Bangladesh (2013) shows a glocal political issue.
items.answer: More than 1,100 garment workers died when a building in Savar collapsed; it supplied global fashion brands, leading to the Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety. a local workplace disaster was tied to global supply chains, and the response involved brands, trade unions and NGOs across borders
items.markingKey: Context (More than 1,100 garment workers died when a building in Savar collapsed; it supplied global fashion brands, leading to the Bangladesh Accord on Fire and Building Safety.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: a local workplace disaster was tied to global supply chains, and the response involved brands, trade unions and NGOs across borders – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to a glocal political issue.

items.stem: Assess the validity of the claim that the individual is the least important level of analysis in global politics.
items.answer: Individuals usually act within structural constraints, but at turning points their choices can be decisive, so the individual level is not negligible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: structural forces (polarity, markets) constrain individuals; states and IGOs have far greater resources. Arguments against: leaders such as Putin or Merkel shaped major decisions; activists such as Malala Yousafzai and Greta Thunberg changed agendas; whistle-blowers such as Edward Snowden altered debates on surveillance. Supported judgement: Individuals usually act within structural constraints, but at turning points their choices can be decisive, so the individual level is not negligible. items.stem: Define the term "intergovernmental organization (IGO)".
items.answer: An organization whose members are states, created by treaty to pursue common goals, such as the UN, WTO or African Union
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an organization whose members are states, created by treaty to pursue common goals, such as the UN, WTO or African Union. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why IGOs depend on their member states.
items.answer: IGOs are created by treaties among states, funded by member contributions and act only within mandates states give them; powerful members (e.g. the P5 in the UN Security Council) can block action.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: IGOs are created by treaties among states, funded by member contributions and act only within mandates states give them; powerful members (e.g. the P5 in the UN Security Council) can block action. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between a social movement and an NGO.
items.answer: A social movement is a loose, often leaderless network of people pursuing change through collective action (e.g. #MeToo); an NGO is a formal organization with staff, budget and legal status (e.g. Oxfam), though NGOs often support movements.
items.markingKey: A social movement is a loose, often leaderless network of people pursuing change through collective action (e.g. #MeToo); an NGO is a formal organization with staff, budget and legal status (e.g. Oxfam), though NGOs often support movements. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: With reference to the International Campaign to Ban Landmines, explain how it illustrates how non-state actors shape international law.
items.answer: A coalition of NGOs worked with like-minded states such as Canada to secure the 1997 Ottawa Treaty; it won the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize. NGOs set the agenda and framed landmines as a humanitarian issue, persuading states to codify a ban outside the usual UN negotiating forum
items.markingKey: Context (A coalition of NGOs worked with like-minded states such as Canada to secure the 1997 Ottawa Treaty; it won the 1997 Nobel Peace Prize.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: NGOs set the agenda and framed landmines as a humanitarian issue, persuading states to codify a ban outside the usual UN negotiating forum – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to how non-state actors shape international law.

items.stem: A government in Southeast Asia wants to stop deforestation by palm-oil companies. Identify one state actor, one non-state actor and one IGO that could be involved, and state one role of each.
items.answer: State: the national government (regulation, licensing); non-state: an NGO such as Greenpeace or WWF (monitoring, campaigns) or a palm-oil MNC (production, certification via RSPO); IGO: ASEAN (regional haze agreement) or UNEP/UNFCCC (climate commitments). 1 mark per actor with role, up to 4.
items.markingKey: State: the national government (regulation, licensing); non-state: an NGO such as Greenpeace or WWF (monitoring, campaigns) or a palm-oil MNC (production, certification via RSPO); IGO: ASEAN (regional haze agreement) or UNEP/UNFCCC (climate commitments). 1 mark per actor with role, up to 4.

items.stem: Analyse how a non-state actor of your choice has influenced a global political issue, and evaluate the limits of its influence.
items.answer: Choose a specific actor (e.g. ICBL, MSF, Greenpeace, Meta). Explain its resources and strategies (expertise, campaigns, litigation, lobbying), give evidence of impact (treaty, policy change) and evaluate limits (state consent, funding, non-signatories such as the US, China and Russia for the Ottawa Treaty).

items.stem: Which of the following documents sets out the four widely cited criteria of statehood?
items.answer: The Montevideo Convention (1933)
items.markingKey: D. Article 1 lists permanent population, defined territory, government and capacity to enter into relations with other states.

items.stem: Explain why MNCs are considered powerful actors in global politics.
items.answer: Their revenues can exceed the GDP of many states, they control investment, jobs and technology, and they can relocate capital, which gives them structural power to shape state policy on tax, labour and regulation.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Their revenues can exceed the GDP of many states, they control investment, jobs and technology, and they can relocate capital, which gives them structural power to shape state policy on tax, labour and regulation. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Non-governmental organizations are always independent of governments." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many NGOs receive significant government funding or work as contractors for aid agencies, and some "GONGOs" are government-organized; independence varies.
items.markingKey: Many NGOs receive significant government funding or work as contractors for aid agencies, and some "GONGOs" are government-organized; independence varies. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Alessia writes: "Social movements always have formal leaders and membership lists." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Many movements, such as the 2019 Hong Kong protests ("be water") or #MeToo, are decentralised networks without formal leaders or membership.
items.markingKey: Many movements, such as the 2019 Hong Kong protests ("be water") or #MeToo, are decentralised networks without formal leaders or membership. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Using Malala Yousafzai's campaign for girls' education as an example, explain the individual as an actor in global politics.
items.answer: After surviving a Taliban assassination attempt in Pakistan in 2012, Malala became a global advocate, co-founded the Malala Fund and won the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize. one person used moral authority and media attention to put girls' education on the global agenda
items.markingKey: Context (After surviving a Taliban assassination attempt in Pakistan in 2012, Malala became a global advocate, co-founded the Malala Fund and won the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: one person used moral authority and media attention to put girls' education on the global agenda – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the individual as an actor in global politics.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"In Sudan the humanitarian response is being kept alive by local mutual-aid groups – the Emergency Response Rooms – while the big agencies negotiate access with armed factions."
— Report on the humanitarian crisis in Sudan, 2024 (adapted)

Identify two types of actor referred to in the source and explain the role of one.
items.answer: Local grassroots/civil society groups (Emergency Response Rooms) and international humanitarian agencies (IGOs/NGOs), plus armed factions (non-state armed groups). E.g. local groups provide food and care where states have collapsed; armed factions control access.
items.markingKey: Local grassroots/civil society groups (Emergency Response Rooms) and international humanitarian agencies (IGOs/NGOs), plus armed factions (non-state armed groups). E.g. local groups provide food and care where states have collapsed; armed factions control access. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "power"?
options: The rightful use of power, accepted as justified by those subject to it
Supreme authority within a territory and independence from external authority
The ability of an actor to achieve its desired outcomes, often by influencing the behaviour of others
A loosely organized, sustained collective effort by people to bring about or resist social or political change, such as Black Lives Matter
items.answer: The ability of an actor to achieve its desired outcomes, often by influencing the behaviour of others
items.markingKey: C. "power" is the ability of an actor to achieve its desired outcomes, often by influencing the behaviour of others.

items.stem: Explain the difference between structural violence and direct violence.
items.answer: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted by an identifiable actor (e.g. armed attack); structural violence is harm built into social and economic structures (e.g. avoidable deaths from poverty) with no single perpetrator.
items.markingKey: Direct violence is physical harm inflicted by an identifiable actor (e.g. armed attack); structural violence is harm built into social and economic structures (e.g. avoidable deaths from poverty) with no single perpetrator. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Identify one example of structural violence in a country of your choice and explain why it fits the concept.
items.answer: E.g. high maternal mortality among poor rural women due to lack of health facilities; it fits because harm results from social and economic structures rather than an individual perpetrator.
items.markingKey: E.g. high maternal mortality among poor rural women due to lack of health facilities; it fits because harm results from social and economic structures rather than an individual perpetrator.

items.stem: Identify which two key concepts are most relevant to the dispute between the EU and member states such as Hungary over the rule of law, and explain why.
items.answer: Sovereignty (Hungary asserts national authority over its judiciary and media) and legitimacy (the EU argues that respect for the rule of law, Article 2 TEU, is a condition of legitimate membership); also power – the EU froze some cohesion funds in 2022.
items.markingKey: Sovereignty (Hungary asserts national authority over its judiciary and media) and legitimacy (the EU argues that respect for the rule of law, Article 2 TEU, is a condition of legitimate membership); also power – the EU froze some cohesion funds in 2022.

items.stem: Discuss how the concepts of conflict, violence and non-violence help to explain a protest movement you have studied.
items.answer: Identify the conflict (interests/values at stake), forms of violence (direct state repression, structural grievances), and non-violent strategies; evaluate outcomes, e.g. Sudan 2019, Belarus 2020 or Myanmar 2021 (shift towards armed resistance after the coup).
items.markingKey: Identify the conflict (interests/values at stake), forms of violence (direct state repression, structural grievances), and non-violent strategies; evaluate outcomes, e.g. Sudan 2019, Belarus 2020 or Myanmar 2021 (shift towards armed resistance after the coup).

items.stem: Explain why peace can be described as more than the absence of war.
items.answer: Following Galtung, a society without war may still suffer structural violence – poverty, discrimination, lack of access to health care – so positive peace requires justice and the removal of these structures.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Following Galtung, a society without war may still suffer structural violence – poverty, discrimination, lack of access to health care – so positive peace requires justice and the removal of these structures. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: "Equality means everyone receiving exactly the same treatment." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Equality can mean formal equality before the law, equality of opportunity or equality of outcome; equity may require different treatment to reach fair outcomes.
items.markingKey: Equality can mean formal equality before the law, equality of opportunity or equality of outcome; equity may require different treatment to reach fair outcomes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe the 2019 Sudanese revolution and explain what it reveals about non-violence as a source of power.
items.answer: Mass, largely non-violent protests led by professional associations and resistance committees led to the removal of Omar al-Bashir in April 2019. unarmed protesters used strikes and sit-ins to delegitimise the regime, showing how non-violent action can shift power
items.markingKey: Context (Mass, largely non-violent protests led by professional associations and resistance committees led to the removal of Omar al-Bashir in April 2019.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: unarmed protesters used strikes and sit-ins to delegitimise the regime, showing how non-violent action can shift power – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to non-violence as a source of power.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"A country with no war but where children die from preventable diseases because clinics are only built in rich neighbourhoods is not at peace in any meaningful sense."
— Peace studies textbook (adapted)

Identify the concept of peace implied in the source and explain it.
items.answer: Positive peace (Galtung): peace requires the absence of structural violence – unequal access to health care is a form of violence built into social structures.
items.markingKey: Positive peace (Galtung): peace requires the absence of structural violence – unequal access to health care is a form of violence built into social structures. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: Assess the validity of the claim that power is the most important key concept for understanding global politics.
items.answer: Power is central but cannot be understood without legitimacy and interdependence; the concepts are interconnected rather than ranked.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every issue involves who controls outcomes; realists see power as the core of politics. Arguments against: legitimacy explains why power is accepted; interdependence and norms shape outcomes without coercion; rights and justice frame many debates. Supported judgement: Power is central but cannot be understood without legitimacy and interdependence; the concepts are interconnected rather than ranked. items.stem: State what is meant by the term "global political issue".
items.answer: An issue whose causes, effects or possible solutions cross state borders and involve actors beyond a single state
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: an issue whose causes, effects or possible solutions cross state borders and involve actors beyond a single state. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "multinational corporation (MNC)"?
options: The processes through which power is exercised and contested and collective decisions are made about who gets what, when and how
The presence of justice, cooperation and the absence of structural violence, not only the absence of war (Johan Galtung)
Freedom of individuals from undue constraint and the ability to make choices about their own lives
A company that owns or controls production or services in more than one country, such as Apple, Shell or Toyota
items.answer: A company that owns or controls production or services in more than one country, such as Apple, Shell or Toyota
items.markingKey: D. "multinational corporation (MNC)" is a company that owns or controls production or services in more than one country, such as Apple, Shell or Toyota.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Freedom of individuals from undue constraint and the ability to make choices about their own lives"?
items.answer: liberty
items.markingKey: C. This is the definition of liberty.

items.stem: Distinguish between the international level of analysis and the national level of analysis.
items.answer: The national level explains outcomes by features inside a state (regime type, institutions, public opinion); the international level explains them by relations between states and the structure of the system (distribution of power, alliances).
items.markingKey: The national level explains outcomes by features inside a state (regime type, institutions, public opinion); the international level explains them by relations between states and the structure of the system (distribution of power, alliances). items.stem: Explain why the concepts of power and legitimacy are closely linked.
items.answer: Power is more stable and less costly when it is seen as legitimate, because people comply willingly rather than through coercion; illegitimate power must rely on force, which is costly and fragile.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Power is more stable and less costly when it is seen as legitimate, because people comply willingly rather than through coercion; illegitimate power must rely on force, which is costly and fragile. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between the international level of analysis and the national level of analysis.
items.answer: The national level explains outcomes by features inside a state (regime type, institutions, public opinion); the international level explains them by relations between states and the structure of the system (distribution of power, alliances).

items.stem: Briefly explain why NGOs can influence states even though they lack military or legal power.
items.answer: NGOs use soft power: expertise, information, moral authority and the ability to mobilise publics and media (naming and shaming). E.g. the International Campaign to Ban Landmines helped secure the 1997 Ottawa Treaty.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: NGOs use soft power: expertise, information, moral authority and the ability to mobilise publics and media (naming and shaming). items.stem: Distinguish between globalization and interdependence.
items.answer: Globalization is the process of increasing worldwide interconnection in trade, communication and culture; interdependence is the resulting condition of mutual dependence, where actors are sensitive or vulnerable to each other's actions.
items.markingKey: Globalization is the process of increasing worldwide interconnection in trade, communication and culture; interdependence is the resulting condition of mutual dependence, where actors are sensitive or vulnerable to each other's actions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A global coffee brand opens 200 cafés in Hanoi, and local independent cafés protest. Outline why this could be studied as a global political issue.
items.answer: It involves power relations between a transnational corporation and local businesses, cultural globalization (homogenisation vs local identity), and possibly state regulation of foreign investment – so causes and effects cross borders.
items.markingKey: It involves power relations between a transnational corporation and local businesses, cultural globalization (homogenisation vs local identity), and possibly state regulation of foreign investment – so causes and effects cross borders.

items.stem: Classify each of the following as an IGO, NGO, MNC or social movement: (a) ASEAN, (b) Oxfam, (c) Shell, (d) #MeToo.
items.answer: (a) IGO; (b) NGO; (c) MNC; (d) social movement. 1 mark each.
items.markingKey: (a) IGO; (b) NGO; (c) MNC; (d) social movement. 1 mark each.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

"Our movement does not carry weapons. Our weapon is the strike, the boycott and the refusal to obey."
— Statement by a civil resistance organiser, 2021 (adapted)

items.answer: Non-violent tactics withdraw cooperation that regimes depend on (labour, consent, revenue), raising the cost of ruling and undermining legitimacy, as in Sudan 2019 or Serbia 2000.

items.stem: A city council in Nairobi debates banning plastic bags, while Kenya joins UN negotiations on a global plastics treaty. Identify two levels of analysis at which this issue can be studied and one actor at each level.

items.stem: Outline one way in which Amazon and Apple in tax disputes with the EU shows the relationship between MNCs and supranational institutions.
items.answer: In 2024 the EU Court of Justice upheld the European Commission's 2016 ruling that Ireland had given Apple illegal state aid, ordering repayment of about €13 billion in taxes. it shows MNCs negotiating favourable tax terms with states, and the EU using supranational legal power to constrain both the MNC and a member state

items.stem: Using South Africa after apartheid as an example, explain the difference between negative and positive peace.
items.answer: Apartheid formally ended with the 1994 elections, but South Africa remains one of the most unequal countries, with a very high Gini coefficient. the end of institutional racial rule did not remove structural inequality, so positive peace remains incomplete

items.answer: Protests forced the Bolivian government to cancel a water privatisation contract with a consortium linked to the US firm Bechtel, after sharp price rises. a local grievance (water prices) was linked to global actors (an MNC, World Bank-backed privatisation), and local people used protest power to reverse the decision

Read the source below.

"Big tech platforms now take decisions on speech that used to belong to parliaments and courts: who may speak, what counts as misinformation, which accounts are removed."
— Opinion column on digital governance, 2022 (adapted)

Explain, with reference to the source, how MNCs may exercise political power.
items.answer: The source argues that platforms make rule-like decisions about speech and access, a function traditionally performed by states; this shows MNCs exercising regulatory and agenda-setting power without democratic accountability.
items.markingKey: The source argues that platforms make rule-like decisions about speech and access, a function traditionally performed by states; this shows MNCs exercising regulatory and agenda-setting power without democratic accountability. Award marks for points drawn explicitly from the source; own knowledge alone is not credited in this part.

items.stem: To what extent is it true that non-violent movements are more effective than violent ones in achieving political change?
items.answer: Evidence suggests non-violent campaigns are more often successful, but success depends on regime type, international support and security force loyalty.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Chenoweth and Stephan found non-violent campaigns (1900–2006) succeeded about twice as often; wider participation and defections from security forces. Arguments against: some non-violent movements were crushed (Tiananmen 1989, Myanmar 2021); violence sometimes achieved independence (Algeria). Supported judgement: Evidence suggests non-violent campaigns are more often successful, but success depends on regime type, international support and security force loyalty. items.stem:
Read the source below.

"What happens in a cobalt mine in the Democratic Republic of Congo is decided as much in boardrooms in Shanghai and California as in Kinshasa. Child labour, local corruption and the global demand for electric-vehicle batteries are parts of the same story."
— Commentary on global supply chains by a development journalist, 2023 (adapted)

With reference to the source, explain why cobalt mining in the DRC can be seen as a global political issue.
items.answer: The source links a local practice (mining, child labour, corruption in the DRC) to global actors and demand (firms in China and the US, the EV market), showing that causes, decisions and effects cross borders and involve state and non-state actors.
items.markingKey: The source links a local practice (mining, child labour, corruption in the DRC) to global actors and demand (firms in China and the US, the EV market), showing that causes, decisions and effects cross borders and involve state and non-state actors. items.stem: With reference to two specific examples you have studied, evaluate the argument that states remain the most important actors in global politics.
items.answer: States remain central because they hold legal authority and coercive power, but on many issues outcomes are shaped jointly with non-state actors, so their importance varies by issue.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: states hold sovereignty, armies and legal authority; IGOs depend on state consent and funding; states regulate MNCs and NGOs. Arguments against: MNCs control capital and technology; NGOs and movements set agendas (Ottawa Treaty, climate); non-state armed groups such as IS controlled territory. Supported judgement: States remain central because they hold legal authority and coercive power, but on many issues outcomes are shaped jointly with non-state actors, so their importance varies by issue. items.stem: Which of the following books by Kenneth Waltz set out three "images" (individual, state, international system) for explaining war?
items.answer: Man, the State and War (1959)
items.markingKey: C. Waltz used three images in 1959; Theory of International Politics (1979) developed structural realism.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Any actor in global politics that is not a state, including IGOs, NGOs, MNCs, social movements, armed groups and individuals"?
items.answer: non-state actor
items.markingKey: A. This is the definition of non-state actor.

items.stem: What best illustrates non-violence as a political strategy?
items.answer: The Salt March led by Mohandas Gandhi in 1930
items.markingKey: The Salt March led by Mohandas Gandhi in 1930. Gandhi's satyagraha used civil disobedience against British colonial rule.

items.stem: "An issue that happens in one village cannot be a global political issue." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Local events can be shaped by and shape global processes – e.g. a mine run by a foreign MNC, or a protest that goes viral – so a local issue can have a global dimension.
items.markingKey: Local events can be shaped by and shape global processes – e.g. a mine run by a foreign MNC, or a protest that goes viral – so a local issue can have a global dimension. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a social movement and an NGO.
items.answer: A social movement is a loose, often leaderless network of people pursuing change through collective action (e.g. #MeToo); an NGO is a formal organization with staff, budget and legal status (e.g. Oxfam), though NGOs often support movements.
items.markingKey: A social movement is a loose, often leaderless network of people pursuing change through collective action (e.g. #MeToo); an NGO is a formal organization with staff, budget and legal status (e.g. Oxfam), though NGOs often support movements. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims that equality means everyone receiving exactly the same treatment. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Equality can mean formal equality before the law, equality of opportunity or equality of outcome; equity may require different treatment to reach fair outcomes.
items.markingKey: Equality can mean formal equality before the law, equality of opportunity or equality of outcome; equity may require different treatment to reach fair outcomes. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Explain why disagreement is central to identifying a political issue.
items.answer: An issue becomes political when actors with different interests or values contest how power, resources or rights should be distributed; if there is no disagreement, there is no need for a collective decision.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: An issue becomes political when actors with different interests or values contest how power, resources or rights should be distributed; if there is no disagreement, there is no need for a collective decision. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: A student claims that conflict always involves violence. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Conflict is a disagreement of interests or values; it can be pursued non-violently through negotiation, courts, protest or elections.

items.stem: Using the COVID-19 pandemic (2020–2023) as an example, explain the interaction of levels of analysis.
items.answer: A virus first identified in Wuhan spread worldwide, leading to border closures, vaccine nationalism and debates about the WHO's authority and the COVAX vaccine-sharing scheme. decisions by individuals, national governments, the WHO and pharmaceutical MNCs all shaped outcomes, showing how a global issue is lived locally
items.markingKey: Context (A virus first identified in Wuhan spread worldwide, leading to border closures, vaccine nationalism and debates about the WHO's authority and the COVAX vaccine-sharing scheme.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) in conflict zones, explain how it illustrates the role of NGOs as non-state actors.
items.answer: MSF provides medical care in places such as Gaza, Sudan and Yemen and publicly denounces attacks on hospitals, e.g. after the 2015 US airstrike on its hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan. MSF delivers services states cannot or will not provide and uses witness testimony to pressure states, showing NGO operational and advocacy power
items.markingKey: Context (MSF provides medical care in places such as Gaza, Sudan and Yemen and publicly denounces attacks on hospitals, e.g. after the 2015 US airstrike on its hospital in Kunduz, Afghanistan.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: With reference to the 2019 Sudanese revolution, explain how it illustrates non-violence as a source of power.
items.answer: Mass, largely non-violent protests led by professional associations and resistance committees led to the removal of Omar al-Bashir in April 2019. unarmed protesters used strikes and sit-ins to delegitimise the regime, showing how non-violent action can shift power

items.stem: Briefly describe the Fridays for Future school strikes started by Greta Thunberg in 2018 and explain what it reveals about how an individual can act at the global level.

items.stem: "Power is the most important key concept for understanding global politics." Discuss.
items.answer: Power is central but cannot be understood without legitimacy and interdependence; the concepts are interconnected rather than ranked.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: every issue involves who controls outcomes; realists see power as the core of politics. Arguments against: legitimacy explains why power is accepted; interdependence and norms shape outcomes without coercion; rights and justice frame many debates. Supported judgement: Power is central but cannot be understood without legitimacy and interdependence; the concepts are interconnected rather than ranked. items.stem: Evaluate the claim that the individual is the least important level of analysis in global politics.
items.answer: Individuals usually act within structural constraints, but at turning points their choices can be decisive, so the individual level is not negligible.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: structural forces (polarity, markets) constrain individuals; states and IGOs have far greater resources. Arguments against: leaders such as Putin or Merkel shaped major decisions; activists such as Malala Yousafzai and Greta Thunberg changed agendas; whistle-blowers such as Edward Snowden altered debates on surveillance. Supported judgement: Individuals usually act within structural constraints, but at turning points their choices can be decisive, so the individual level is not negligible. items.stem: "Non-governmental organizations have more legitimacy than governments when speaking about human rights." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: NGOs often have strong expertise-based legitimacy, but they lack democratic legitimacy, so their authority depends on accuracy and impartiality.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: NGOs are independent and evidence-based; they lack the self-interest of states. Arguments against: NGOs are unelected and may reflect donor or Western priorities; governments have democratic mandates and legal responsibility. Supported judgement: NGOs often have strong expertise-based legitimacy, but they lack democratic legitimacy, so their authority depends on accuracy and impartiality.
